source.title: How Should LLMs Consume High-Quality Data? Optimal Data Scheduling via Quality-Aware Functional Scaling Laws
source.authors: Zhitao Zhu; Xili Wang; Shizhe Wu; Jiawei Fu; Xiaoqing Liu

record.tranche_reason: Uses functional scaling laws to derive a data-quality and batch-size scheduling method, then evaluates that method. It does not test the claim versions about language-model pretraining loss scaling, compute-optimal parameter/token allocation, or predictability from scaling-law fits.
record.gate_note: The paper verifies a quality-aware excess-risk law in a feature-space regression simulation, including excess risk versus data budget. These results are not held-out pretraining loss measurements from language models. The LLM experiments compare batch-size and learning-rate schedules using downstream benchmark accuracy, not loss-versus-parameters/tokens/compute scaling or scaling-law extrapolation.
record.test_reason: The paper extends functional scaling laws (Li et al.) to time-varying data quality, derives optimal quality/batch schedules, and evaluates its own Drop-Stable-Rampup schedule on LLM midtraining by benchmark accuracy. Its only scaling-type measurements are excess risk versus data budget in a synthetic linear-regression model with power-law spectra. That is not held-out LM pretraining loss versus parameters, tokens or compute. There is no extrapolation test, no compute-optimal N/D allocation, no architecture-shape sweep, and no downstream-vs-scale predictability test. LLM results compare schedules at fixed model size and token budget.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that data quality and batch size should be scheduled jointly. Low batch after a quality transition accumulates signal; late high-quality placement and a terminal batch ramp-up suppress noise. Drop-Stable-Rampup beat WSD and Cosine in their midtraining experiments: +1.70 over WSD on the 15B MoE, and +3.27 and +5.25 over the best baseline on the public-data dense and MoE models.
record.recipe_differences: The paper extends functional scaling laws to time-varying data quality and batch size, then evaluates a midtraining schedule. It does not use the parameter/token/compute sweeps or held-out pretraining-loss fits in the original scaling-law claims.
record.method_sensitivity: Results vary with noise-limited versus signal-limited regime and, in LLM experiments, with the downstream benchmark and stable-phase ratio.

fits_no_version.finding: In synthetic feature-space regression, measured excess-risk trajectories track the quality-aware FSL prediction across Early, Late, Middle and Sinusoidal schedules. This holds in both regimes (noise-limited s = 2; signal-limited s = 0.4).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Quality-aware functional scaling laws track SGD excess-risk dynamics under time-varying data quality and batch size in linear regression.

fits_no_version.finding: Under joint-optimal schedules, final excess risk follows predicted power laws in data budget: −0.81 vs −0.80 (noise-limited) and −0.51 vs −0.50 (signal-limited). Suboptimal strategies show shallower scaling.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In linear-regression models, the data-scaling exponent of excess risk depends on the quality/batch schedule; joint-optimal schedules attain the theoretical exponent.

record.problems: The paper notes that its theory uses feature-space linear regression with Gaussian features and power-law spectral decay, rather than nonlinear LLM dynamics. Its LLM experiments cover only a 600M dense model and a 15B-total/2.4B-active MoE model, and the authors do not establish universal transfer. Comparisons are token-budget matched rather than wall-clock matched; low-batch schedules incur reported wall-clock overhead. The LLM results do not measure pretraining loss scaling or test scaling-law extrapolation.
record.rows_left_out: No rows for LLM schedule comparisons and downstream benchmark scores: those compare training schedules and report accuracy, not a result measuring any listed scaling-law version. No numerical risk values were extracted from Figure 5; the figure-only trajectory comparisons are recorded as such.

untested.parts: No LM pretraining loss measured against parameters, tokens or compute.
No small-to-large extrapolation of fitted laws.
No parameter/token allocation under a compute budget; optimizes batch and quality schedules only.
No depth/width variation at fixed parameter count.
Midtraining compared only across schedules; no scaling-law form tested in midtraining or other modalities.
Benchmark accuracy compared across schedules at fixed scale; no predictability from scale or loss.

No comparison of fitted exponents across fitting or setup choices for LMs. The synthetic result that suboptimal schedules show shallower data-scaling exponents bears only loosely on schedule dependence of exponents.

record.verdict_notes: The record's classification as T4/uses_without_test is right. The stable-ratio sweep reports LM validation loss (MMLU/CMMLU) against stable-phase ratio at fixed size and budget. That is a schedule-selection value, not a scaling measurement, so leaving it out of the rows is fine.

versions.untested_parts: Does not test held-out LLM pretraining loss as a function of parameters, tokens, or compute.
Does not fit scaling laws on small LLM runs and compare predictions with larger runs.
Optimizes data quality and batch size for a data budget in a theoretical model; does not test parameter/token allocation as a function of compute.
Does not vary architecture details at fixed parameter count to measure their effect on loss.
The LLM midtraining experiments compare schedules but do not test whether the same loss power law holds in midtraining or other regimes.
Reports downstream accuracy under different schedules, but does not test whether downstream performance is predictable from scale or pretraining loss.
Does not compare fitted exponents or allocation laws across fitting choices, or test whether scaling curves bend away from power laws.
